key_concept: All chordates share four fundamental features at some stage of life: a notochord, a dorsal hollow nerve cord, paired pharyngeal gill slits, and a post-anal tail.
steps: Recall the four fundamental chordate characters: (i) a notochord, (ii) a dorsal, hollow, single nerve cord, (iii) paired pharyngeal gill slits, and (iv) a post-anal tail.
Option (1), presence of notochord: this is the defining chordate feature. It is a true characteristic.
Option (2), dorsal central nervous system: chordates have a dorsal hollow nerve cord, whereas non-chordates have a ventral, solid one. It is a true characteristic.

Option (3), absence of gills: chordates have pharyngeal gill slits at least in the embryo, even when adults (such as mammals) lack gills. Absence of gills is therefore not a chordate characteristic. In fact, gill slits are absent in non-chordates.
Option (4), post-anal tail: a post-anal part is present in all chordates at some stage. It is a true characteristic.
Only option (3) contradicts the chordate plan, so the answer is (3).
why_not_others: Options (1), (2) and (4) each describe one of the fundamental chordate features. Only 'absence of gills' is a non-chordate feature, because chordates have pharyngeal gill slits at least in the embryo.
common_trap: Students think of adult mammals or birds, which have no gills, and wrongly treat 'absence of gills' as true for chordates. They forget that pharyngeal gill slits appear in every chordate embryo.
time_saving_tip: Memorise the four chordate hallmarks (notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal gill slits, post-anal tail). Any option that negates one of them is the odd one out.
